projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Chester Wasileski was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Can you please state your name and your birth date.

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Okay. My name is Chester Wasileski, birth date is November 13th, 1921.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Which war or wars did you fight in?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Okay. I was in World War II.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: And where were you stationed during the war?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Okay. I was stationed in several places, but in the U.S. I was stationed mostly in the South, and then I went overseas -- I just looked it up -- 1944, and I went to New Guinae. And then from New Guinae, I went to the Philippines. And from the Philippines, I went to Okinawa. And from Okinawa, I went home. That was in 19 -- as soon as the war was over, I got out.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Were you drafted, or did you enlist in the military?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: No. I enlisted. I enlisted in 1940, before the war started.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Why did you join the service to begin with?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Well, it is a pretty easy story to answer. I graduated from high school in 1939. I didn't have money to go to college. I had been brought up on a farm. And my dad didn't like farming any more than I did, and he sold the farm. He -- he built a filling station and a garage. You know, I might repeat a little bit. I finished high school in 1939, which was toward the end of the depression. As I say, I grew up on a farm, and my dad sold the farm. When things perked up again, he bought -- built the filling station and a garage sort of combination, like garage work. And so I finished high school. And I couldn't find any work, so I was working with my dad, and it didn't seem to be too good of a deal, so a bunch of us decided to go in the service. My sister was married to a serviceman, so I knew a little bit about it. I used to go visit them at the base that he was posted _____+ or something like that. And I liked airplanes, so I decided to join the -- at that time it was called the Army Air Corps. So we went down with me and a group of guys, three or four or five of us, we would have had a basketball team, our own basketball team. A whole bunch of us decided to go join the -- join the Army Air Corps. So, anyway, I went down, and they said, "Well, we could send you -- you can to the Philippines or you can go to Panama." I said, "I don't like either one of those," so the deal was off. It was about a week or two later they called me and said would I like to go to Mitchel Field in Long Island, and I said that would be fine. So -- and that was in 1940 sometime _____+. So I went to Mitchel Field. Anyway, that's how I got in. There was no work around; I went in the Army. And that wasn't very good either, 21 bucks a month.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Where were you living at that time before you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Well, where I went in -- I went in from Richfield Springs, New York, which was in the central New York area. I was born in Utica and lived on a farm in Madison. I finished high school in Madison. My family lived in Richfield Springs. That's where I was from.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Tell me something interesting that happened to you during this time, when you first joined.

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Well, the interesting thing when I first joined was that -- first of all, the pay was 21 dollars a month, which was okay, but then they took out money for your laundry, took out money for the soldiers' home and all so you had, like, 15 dollars a month left. Now, it doesn't sound like much money nowadays, and it wasn't much money then, but it was something. Because you got -- you got all your clothes, you get your food, you get your _____. So, well, the other thing is I guess I hadn't been in the service, but I guess when they sent me down to Mitchel Field in Long Island from Utica, I think we rode the train all night or something. They picked us up on a truck and took us out near Mitchel Field on Long Island out in New York City. Went out up there I guess -- it was cold, they gave us a whole bunch of clothing and barracks and stuff to carry and bedding. And said, okay, took us to the barracks, showed us how to make up the bed, and made up the bed Army style, which is still the way they make beds today. And then they said, "Okay, you are on KP." KP, in case you don't know, it is called kitchen police. So you have to scrub the pots and pans and help to cook and help carry the food to the table, peel the potatoes, and do the _____ that kind of stuff. Well, I didn't like that very well, so like I was ready to get out. That was it, one day I was ready to get out. But it was five years later. But it got a little better after that. I don't know. Anyway, I wasn't too crazy about it. Then they sent me to school after taking the fitness exam. Well, you had a like six weeks, five- or six-week basic training _____+. Then they -- you took some exams. And then depending on what grade you had in your exams, you could pick out what kind of school you wanted to go to _____+, go be a mechanic or radio operator or weather forecaster or control tower operator, sheet metal, things of that nature. I chose radio. So they shunt me to Scott Field in Illinois for a basic kind of mechanic's course there. I was only -- I was only supposed to be there about a month, I was supposed to be there a month, but four of the people in our barracks got the measles so we got -- we missed part of the class to move on, we were supposed to move on to _____. We got delayed there anyway. Then I did go _____+. And lo and behold, while I was there, they decided to move the regular school back to Scott Field _____. So I spent -- I don't know how long I was supposed to be in the school, but I was there about twice as long as I was supposed to be. Then I went to McDonough Field (ph).

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Do you still have contact with any other men that served with you during that time?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Do I? Well, yeah, I did, but most of them are gone. The ones that I served with in the United States _____+ good friends. Red Hogan, he lived in Mississippi. We used to see him, in fact, when we lived in Huntsville. When Alabama would play -- would play University of Mississippi they used to be played either in Tuscaloosa or in Jackson, Mississippi. He lived near Jackson, so we would always swap back and forth _____+ was a weak spot. But then one day, we were out west, and in fact we were on a trip with your mom and dad. We had been to Branson _____+ and we had to come home early. We left them at Branson, we had to come home early. And we went through Jackson, and we were going to stop to see Hogan. When I called, his wife answered the phone, said he had been dead for a year, so -- then another friend -- in fact, a guy -- a man named Max Willingham was the reason I came to Alabama from New York was this, when we came -- we were in the service together when we split apart when we were overseas, and I knew he was in the Pacific the same time I was. But then when we got ready to come home, I happened to be in Japan, or in Korea, Seol, Korea at the time I got orders to come home. My ship was leaving the next day or something _____+ Philippines _____+ to Okinawa. And this guy, Max Willingham, was in my tent waiting for me, because he was on the same ship coming home. And that's when I made the deal with him coming home, they said, well, we would go -- we were going to go to New Orleans, go to the Sugar Bowl Game. That was in '45, so it would be New Year's Day '46 Sugar Bowl. Well, I got malaria in December, so I couldn't come then. But after I got over the malaria, we missed the Sugar Bowl Game, but I came on down later. And he's the one that introduced _____. So I had already decided I was going to go to -- well, I was going to go to Cornell or _____+. Well, I got down there and _____+. But I had good grades in high school. In fact, I was valedictorian of my high school class, and he did go onto school at the _____+. So she called in and lo and behold got in. So that's one of the -- you don't talk about people. But I called him one day, because his family lived in -- his family lived in Tuscaloosa. And we had gone there for the fairs. And I called him one day. Lo and behold, his brother answered the phone, he's been dead about a year or so. A lot of the people that I served with are gone. Now, one of the outfits that I was with was called 84th (Airborne Squad?) which I was with _____+. They have a reunion about every year. So I have been to one or two reunions. The reunions are getting pretty small. In fact, there's going to be one in October this year. It is going to be in St. Augustine _____+. A lot of the people that come now are wives or something. The World War II veterans are disappearing. Well, your grandfather's gone.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: What was your rank upon exiting the service?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: I was a master sergeant, which is the highest enlisted rank.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Did you move up to like _____+?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Yeah, I started as a private. Well, in the Army, Air Force, Air Corps, whichever it was, they had -- they had a special deal, like, I don't know if you know the ranks, you know, there's private, there's corporal, and sergeant, staff sergeant, tech sergeant, master sergeant. They had a -- and they had a deal where after you went to school, you could take an exam, and you could become something called an air mechanic, air mechanic first class, air mechanic second class. And they got the same pay as a -- like a tech sergeant, which is the next-to-the-highest pay. So I took the exam, passed it, so I was -- even though I was a corporal, I was getting the tech sergeant's pay. There was a downside to that, too, because you couldn't get flying pay. Flying pay -- because I was always in flight status, 9 flight crews. Flying pay gives you fifty percent extra. So if you made 100 dollars a month, if you were on flight status you would get 150 dollars per month _____+. Then when I got to be staff sergeant, I dropped that because the pay was higher. Well, anyway I was a master sergeant.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Did you receive any honors or medals during your time -- your time in the service?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Well, I just listed them on that other thing there, just Philippine liberation, good conduct medal. I don't know, some others not too extensive, just for being around. I didn't get any Purple Hearts or -- although, I was very sick but _____+. I was very sick with malaria _____+. I had malaria for quite a while after I served. In fact, I got disability _____ for a while.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: When you exited the service, did they tell you you were done, or did you -- can you make that decision when you become master sergeant or --

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: No. They want you to stay in. Of course, you didn't have any choice. During the war, you had no choice. You were there, you were there. And when -- as soon as the war was over -- what you did, what you did when you were in the service, you got points. And supposedly when you got 75 or 80 points or something, you were eligible for discharge, but they didn't let anybody go during the war unless _____+ you have to stay in for the duration. Well, I had signed up for three years, which I stayed the duration. But you got points when you were overseas in certain points for certain areas and combat missions and this and that, you got points. You know, like 85 points you were eligible, at least we'll take back to the States, which they never did, they just kept you, or at least -- I don't know, I had 100 and some odd points. So as soon as the war ended, well, I was going to come home. _____+ went to Fort Dix, and they -- they only kept you there a little while to process you. They said if you join the reserves, you know, you could go home right now, but -- so I stayed about three or four days, free and clear.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: What did your family think at the time you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: I don't know. They probably felt it was a good thing. I'm not sure. I'm sure my mom didn't care too much about it. My dad probably didn't either because I was hanging around there working with him. I think he was all right with it. They were all right. They had a son-in-law who was _____+. The war wasn't going. There was no war. It is different if there's a war.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Well, how did you stay in contact with them, though, when the war did start? Did you -- were you able to contact them while you were overseas or while you were away?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I used to write. Of course, we didn't have e-mail and we couldn't telephone. I'd just write. They had a -- we used to call it _____+, just write. And then they'd send me packages when I was overseas, sent me packages. In fact, my dad used to send me -- he used to take Listerine bottles and fill them with liquor and stuff, too. But it was against the law, I guess, so he always put it in a Listerine bottle. Then mom sent cookies, and they sent me canned meat, like, and stuff, _____+.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Tell me about your training, where you actually fought in the war.

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Training. That's all -- that's all you do in the service is train. Well, as I said, I went to radio school, and I became a radio operator. And then I was flying all over the country. I was stationed at (McDonough?) Field. Just flight training. That's all you do. That's all you do in the service, you train. That's why I say when there's no war, I don't know what these people do. They train forever. That's -- They have nothing else to do but train. And so we just -- well, I was on flight status, and as I say, I flew all over the country, used to make cross-country trips. One particular trip that's pretty interesting is this man was a major, he was _____+ up to North Dakota, and this is a training mission, but that's where he was from; that's where his family lived. We landed in a pasture in North Dakota. And he visited with his family, and I stayed with his family, and came back, and came back home. But, you know, that's all you did was just practice. I was in training, is all I can say.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Do you remember what was going on in the world just before and after the war?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Before and after? Yeah. I knew about the war going on in Europe _____+. And then after, of course, yeah, I was pretty well _____+. When we were overseas, we had, like, it happened when they dropped the nuclear bomb, you know. In fact, I flew over afterward. I flew over Nagasaki after the second bomb. But, yeah, we used to listen to the radio, and Air Force Armed Services radio. And I was flying between Okinawa and the Philippines, and I heard on the radio two things happened up there. One, they dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima. And the second piece of news there was a guy named Richard Balm (ph) who was a fighting pilot, one of the fighter pilots. And he was at the same base that I was at. He had flown back to the States _____+. He got killed in a training flight. So I was well aware of the news all the time, to what was going on in the war and mainly like the overseas _____+.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Do you remember the reaction to the President _____?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Did you _____+ on the radio?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Well, yeah. We were up to date on news, mostly through Armed Forces short wave radio. I being a radio operator, I was listening to it all the time.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Has there been a change in anything where you ____+?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: There was no difference as far as I was concerned. No.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: What is it like actually fighting in a war?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Well, I don't know. I didn't have to do any fighting. I mean, we just -- the only thing I ever did was flew a few bombing missions or recognizance missions. So, you know, it is not like fighting on the ground, hand to hand and shooting. And the only thing we got bombed a couple of times, just almost just a single _____+. Well, at one time -- see, I really didn't fight. I mean, I can't say, but we had some scares a few times, you know, some bombs dropping on us. One time -- I'm trying to think. This was in -- this was in the Philippines. We were stationed up at the top of Logan, and there was a Japanese like suicide airplane came in there, landed on the airstrip, and a bunch of guys got out, and they were going to try _____+. They didn't get very far. The ground troops got them. But our guys were all kind of scared because we weren't used to that kind of stuff. We weren't used to Japanese people being around us and _____+ or something. So only incidents like that. One time we were based down where the ships were unloading supplies, and there was a Japanese bomber _____+. They used to send -- they used to send these planes out at -- I won't tell you what we called them -- at night just so you would sound the alarm so you wouldn't sleep. The alarms would wake you up, you'd have to get up. After a while _____+ just to keep you awake, they were harassing you, the planes were. In fact, we used to call them _____ Charlies. We called these guys _____+. So as far as, you know, fighting, no.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: What was your best and worst during that time?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Best and worst. Best was when the war was over and I was going home. That was for sure the best. My worst. The worst was sometime, because the medical facilities were not all that good, they were not near as good as you see on that show they had, you know, about the Korean War. If you got sick, it was really bad if you got sick. I had Dengue fever one time, it was very, very _____ some of that -- so I'd say when you got a fever, you got sick or something was the worst situation.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: How were the hospital areas and stuff that took care of you at that time?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Lousy. Not near as good as you see on these television shows where they show them so rudimentary and they have all these _____+ and stuff. It was not like that. I remember one time -- dental, dental. I just had trouble with my teeth, and the Army pulled some teeth, which they probably shouldn't have done. But when I got overseas, the dental drills they had a thing like, you know, like a hole to thread a sewing machine, they had a thing like that to drill your teeth with. And you couldn't get in to the dentist. You had to take _____. I made a deal -- I traded -- I went down to the dentist people, I traded them some Olympic motors we had on some Teletype machines which we were using, I put them on those drills so they didn't have to pedal them and drill, and they had a nice constant speed and all. And the dentists were real happy about that, so I got my teeth fixed for that. But the facilities were pretty poor.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: Why did you pick this area of service you joined into? And now would you think of another, or another -- another branch of the service that you would be interested in, or would you still pick the Air Force?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: No. If I was going to go back, I'd be Air Force because that's what I was interested in. I would not -- I would never -- I would not have volunteered. Well, there's another thing. When I was in there, they came around one time doing some exams _____+, the Army had so many people they didn't know what to do about it. So then they was going to send _____+. So they came out, took some exams again, said you are eligible, you can go to college. Well, then I thought about it. I said, well, I am really not going to do -- never going to _____+. I'm kind of glad I didn't, because I know some people, some that worked for me later on here at Kennedy, that went and joined that program. In fact, one guy he had gone through, he was there about four or five months or six months and they decided, well, I don't know why they terminated the program or what, but then they put him in the infantry and sent him over to Europe, and he was in the Battle of the Bulge. Now, if I had chosen that route, that's where I might have wound up, Tom McCarmody (ph) is his name, that's what happened to him.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: After the war, what did you do, and how did you end up to come here in Florida?

sp.speaker: Chester Wasileski
sp.p: Well, after the war, I went to school, of course, University of Alabama. The reason I went there you know. So when I finished, I went to work at -- in fact, _____+ kind of scared me, I finished college in '49. High school '39, college '49. So in any case, then I went to college, I went to work at Pratt and Whitney, because they worked aircraft engines, and I liked those engines. So I went to work there. I was there for two, three years. And my family at that time moved to Miami. _____ family was in Alabama. So anytime we got two, three weeks off, we'd just come to the south. So we came down one time, and we came to Tuscaloosa and some of my friends were still in college, and they said you are hired _____+ that's all about. So I went up there, and then I found out they had these Germans that could come you know after the war and start the rocket program and all. So I talked to them, and I got hired there, went to -- went back to Pratt and Whitney, gave them a notice, and we moved down to Huntsville in 19 -- that was 1951. So we moved to Huntsville, that's where I met your dad and mom. And the kids were born about the same as our kids, the same time _____+. So that's how we got to Huntsville. Then we got to -- we got to Florida because we were transferred when they consolidated, and then we switched in to NASA, and then _____+. That's how we wound up in Florida.

sp.speaker: Callie Sparkman
sp.p: All right. Well, sounds good. Thank you so much for giving me the interview. {CONCLUSION OF INTERVIEW}
